question: A recent study published in the press highlights that offshore wind farms can alter surface wind, reduce vertical mixing and significantly increase the sea surface temperature, potentially impacting marine biodiversity and fishery resources.

Meanwhile, the Commission is strongly encouraging the large-scale deployment of offshore wind, even though such energy is intermittent, weather-dependent and difficult to store, requires costly back-up capacity, and receives significant public subsidies, which are likely to distort competition, and even to go hand in hand with dumping practices, particularly in the face of the almost monopolistic imports of equipment.
In light of the precautionary principle and marine protection targets, can the Commission: 1.
reassess its quantitative targets and financial support for offshore wind?
consider redirecting some of those resources towards controllable, low-carbon and nonweather-dependent electricity production, such as nuclear power?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.3.2026) To deliver more affordable and secure energy to all Europeans and achieve the decarbonisation objectives as enshrined in the European Climate Law target (taking into account the precautionary principle)1, the Union needs to significantly scale up renewable electricity generation.

As clearly stated in the Hamburg Declaration during the North Sea Summit on 26 January 2026, offshore renewable generation contributes to enhance Europe’s energy resilience, provide affordable energy to consumers and ensure long-term competitiveness of European industries. In December 2024, Member States themselves updated their goals on offshore renewable energy.

Their combined figures result in an overall ambition of installing approximately 360 gigawatts by 2050. Indeed, all net-zero and low carbon technologies will need to contribute to reach the climate goals. This includes all current and future solutions such as i.a. renewables, nuclear, and carbon removals2. Offshore renewables are an indispensable part of the energy mix.

In line with the precautionary principle and EU environmental laws, it is essential to carry out an assessment of the likely environmental effects of certain projects likely to have significant effects on the environment, including on offshore renewable energy, before a permit is granted.

The financial support at EU level is based on legislative acts on EU funds, such as Horizon Europe3, the Connecting Europe Facility4 and the Innovation Fund5. Funding awards are subject to project application, and independent scrutiny based on objective criteria.
1 2021/1119/EU; see Articles 2 and 4, and preamble paragraph (9) (https://eur-

lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/1119/oj/eng). 2 Interinstitutional File 2025/0524 (COD) 19 December 2025, preamble paragraph (5) (https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-17086-2025-INIT/en/pdf).
